stances.claim: SALN omissions constitute dismissal when they amount to dishonesty; mere clerical errors in good faith result only in suspension or fine.

In impeachment, the Senate has wider policy discretion than the strict legality applied in SC administrative cases -- it decides whether the respondent is still fit and qualified as the highest magistrate.
stances.rhetorical_move: closing distinction between administrative and impeachment standards

notable_anecdotes: Rabe v. Flores: an RTC interpreter dismissed for omitting a market stall from her SALN -- the most minor property imaginable, yet treated as serious dishonesty warranting dismissal.
Pleyto v. PNP-CIDG: a police officer spared from dismissal because he relied on a family bookkeeper and his SALNs 'actually disclosed the full extent of his assets' -- the good-faith safety valve.
OCA v. Usman: the counterintuitive hierarchy -- failure to file SALN at all (2004-2008) penalized with only a P5,000 fine, while dishonest omission of specific assets draws dismissal.

decision_framework_signals: Test SALN omissions for dishonesty vs clerical error: dishonesty (intent to conceal) → dismissal; good faith clerical error → suspension/fine
Apply RA 6713 Sec. 11(b): administrative penalty does not require criminal prosecution

one_paragraph_summary: Responding to reader questions about the penalty for SALN omissions charged in Article II of the Corona impeachment, Panganiban synthesizes five SC cases. The baseline rule: RA 6713 Sec. 8 requires a sworn SALN as a check-and-balance tool; Sec. 11(b) prescribes removal even without criminal prosecution. Rabe v. Flores (1997) dismissed an RTC interpreter for omitting a market stall; Concerned Taxpayer v. Doblada (2005) dismissed an RTC sheriff for years of SALN discrepancies; Flores v. Montemayor (2011) dismissed a respondent who failed to declare two expensive cars. The mitigating exception: Pleyto v. PNP-CIDG (2007) imposed only a 6-month suspension when the respondent acted in simple negligence without bad faith and his SALNs actually disclosed the full extent of assets. OCA v. Usman (2011) imposed a P5,000 fine for five years of non-filing -- showing that failure to disclose dishonestly is penalized more severely than mere non-filing. The synthesis: dishonesty in SALN = dismissal; clerical errors in good faith = suspension or fine. Ombudsman v. Peliño (2008) defines dishonesty as 'a disposition to lie, cheat, deceive, or defraud.' The column closes by noting that in impeachment, the Senate has wider policy discretion than SC administrative cases -- it decides whether the respondent remains fit as the highest magistrate.
